text: Few scientific advances have proven as profound as our newfound ability to manipulate the human genome. Techniques that once seemed the stuff of science fiction now allow researchers to splice faulty sequences and, at least in theory, eradicate hereditary diseases before a child is even born. Proponents argue that such tools could safeguard future generations from suffering long associated with genetic mutation. Skeptics, however, warn that tampering with the genome carries risks that are not merely inherent but potentially irreversible. Were an unforeseen consequence to emerge only after the technology had already taken root in clinical practice, there would be little means of undoing the damage. Nor is the debate purely scientific: it is deeply ethical, touching on questions of consent, inequality, and what it means to be human. A troubling discrepancy has also emerged between wealthy nations racing to adopt these methods and poorer countries left without access altogether. Governments must now decide how best to mitigate the dangers looming over this controversial frontier, albeit without stifling research that could, ultimately, save countless lives.
